text: Chapter three, the system design interview framework. Let's see how it works in four minutes.

A system design interview lasts forty-five minutes, so you can't just answer whatever comes to mind. The book gives a four-step framework: understand the problem, design at a high level, dive deep, and wrap up. A typical split is eight minutes, twelve, twenty, and five.

Step one: don't draw yet. Ask questions. A good question changes the design. If the feed is just reverse chronological, you don't need a recommender. The number of friends decides how many people each post fans out to. Images and video mean object storage and a CDN.

Then write your assumptions down. If you have no numbers, propose a starting value and invite the interviewer to correct it. For example: I'll design for ten million users, far more reads than writes, sorted by time. Is that scope okay? By minute ten, you should have requirements and the core API.

Step two: draw a high-level blueprint, and treat the interviewer as a teammate. Boxes for the client, the API, the database, and the cache. Then do a back-of-the-envelope estimate to check the design can cope. Finally, walk two flows. Publishing writes the post and fills friends' feeds. Retrieval gathers friends' posts and shows them newest first.

Step three: dig only into the most critical bottleneck. Take a celebrity post, which fans out to a huge audience. Say inbox updates are processed at twenty thousand per second, but thirty thousand arrive. In one minute, six hundred thousand pile up. Adding stateless API servers won't help. Raise processing capacity, or change the fan-out strategy.

While digging, ask yourself four questions. What are the key and the access pattern? What are the capacity limits and failure modes? What if data is lost, duplicated, or delayed? And when do you upgrade? The answer lands on a trade-off. Regular users get push on write, for fast reads. Celebrities get merge on read, accepting extra read work.

Step four: wrap up. In the last five minutes, add no new components. Minute one: restate the goals and assumptions. Minute two: walk the write and read paths. Minute three: trade-offs. Minute four: bottlenecks and failures. Minute five: upgrade triggers. After minute forty, stop adding components.

Now the common pitfalls along this timeline. At the start, you draw a wall of buzzwords before locking the scope. In the middle, you burn time on table columns and class names, and skip hotspots, timeouts, and retries. At the end, you're still adding components, with no wrap-up. The fixes: ask more, don't go silent, stay focused, avoid over-engineering.

With only ninety seconds, you can still chain the four steps. Requirements, fifteen seconds. Paths, twenty-five. Bottleneck, fifteen. Trade-offs, twenty. Evolution, fifteen. In one line: who needs what, how a request flows, where it jams first, why accept the cost, and what evidence triggers an upgrade.

To sum up. Clarify the scope, get buy-in, then close on trade-offs. The interview isn't about memorizing one universal architecture. It's about showing how you make decisions with incomplete information.
